title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 162 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 789–791 (Night 162, continuing directly from nights-161), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 162 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. At the jeweller's house Shams al-Nahār finishes speaking: nothing is gained without effort, the jeweller now holds their secret, and her slave-girl, keeper of her secrets, will carry word of ʿAlī between them through him. When she has gone he goes to ʿAlī, who has not slept since they parted and has heard from the girl already. The jeweller laughs at his distress; ʿAlī reproaches him in verse, then listens, changing colour, to all that has happened, and begs his help. The jeweller proposes that the lovers meet at his own house, the place Shams al-Nahār chose, and sits up with ʿAlī until morning. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-sittūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second-and-sixty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixty-second night,
sentences.n: Built as last night's heading was: al-thāniya, “the second”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-sittūn, “and the sixty”; then baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”. The alif of المائة is silent: the word is miʾa.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ قَالَتْ لِلْجَوْهَرِيِّ لَا تَحْصُلُ رَاحَةٌ إِلَّا بَعْدَ تَعَبٍ وَلَا يَظْهَرُ نَجَاحٌ إِلَّا مِنْ ذِى مُرُوَّةٍ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Shamsa al-Nahāri qālat li-al-jawhariyyi lā taḥṣulu rāḥatun illā baʿda taʿabin wa-lā yaẓharu najāḥun illā min dhī murūwatin
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Shams al-Nahār said to the jeweller: No rest comes-about except after toil, and no success appears except from one-possessed-of manly-virtue.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Shams al-Nahār said to the jeweller, “No rest is had except after toil, and no success comes except from a man of honour.
sentences.n: The print runs al-saʿīd and anna together as one word (السعيدان); the spacing is kept here and the word is read as the two it stands for. Shams al-Nahār takes up the saying she spoke at the close of last night, lā … illā, “no … except”, and adds a second clause to it. dhū, “possessor of”, here in the genitive after min (printed ذى): “one who has”. murūwa, “manliness, chivalry, generous honour”, the sum of a gentleman's virtues; the shadda of مروّة is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ أَطْلَعْتُكَ الْآنَ عَلَى أَمْرِنَا وَصَارَ بِيَدِكَ هَتْكُنَا وَسَتْرُنَا وَلَا زِيَادَةَ لِمَا أَنْتَ عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمُرُوَّةِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad aṭlaʿtuka al-āna ʿalā amrinā wa-ṣāra bi-yadika hatkunā wa-satrunā wa-lā ziyādata li-mā anta ʿalayhi mina al-murūwati
sentences.l: And I-have-informed-you now of our-affair, and our-exposing and our-veiling have-come-to-be in-your-hand; and there-is-no adding to what you (are) upon of the manly-virtue.
sentences.i: Now I have let you into our secret, and it lies in your hand to shame us or to shield us; and no man could have more honour than you have.
sentences.n: aṭlaʿa ʿalā (Form IV), “to let someone see, acquaint him with”. hatk, “tearing (a veil), disgracing”, and satr, “veiling, keeping hidden”, are a rhyming pair: “our exposure and our protection”. lā ziyādata, the lā that denies a whole class, its noun accusative without tanwīn: “there is no adding to”. mā anta ʿalayhi, “what you are upon”, the state or character one has. The madda of الآن is the print's own; it writes المروة here without the shadda it gave مروّة just before.

sentences.t: فَأَنْتَ قَدْ عَلِمْتَ أَنَّ جَارِيَتِي هَذِهِ كَاتِمَةٌ لِسِرِّي وَبِسَبَبِ ذَلِكَ لَهَا رُتْبَةٌ عَظِيمَةٌ عِنْدِى وَقَدِ اخْتَصَصْتُهَا لِمُهِمَّاتِ أُمُورِي
sentences.tr: fa-anta qad ʿalimta anna jāriyatī hādhihi kātimatun li-sirrī wa-bi-sababi dhālika lahā rutbatun ʿaẓīmatun ʿindī wa-qadi ikhtaṣaṣtuhā li-muhimmāti umūrī
sentences.l: So you have-come-to-know that this slave-girl-of-mine (is) a-concealer of-my-secret, and by-reason of that to-her (is) a great rank with-me; and I-have-singled-her-out for the weighty-ones of my-affairs.
sentences.i: You know already that this slave-girl of mine keeps my secrets, and for that she stands high in my regard; I have chosen her for all my weightiest business.
sentences.n: kātima li-sirrī, “a keeper of my secret”: the active participle takes its object through li-. ikhtaṣṣa (Form VIII) with li-, “to single out, set apart for”; before a consonantal ending the doubled ṣād is written out in full, اختصصتها. muhimmāt, “matters of importance”. The shadda of لسرّي is the print's own; عندى is its spelling of ʿindī.

sentences.t: فَلَا يَكُنْ عِنْدَكَ أَعَزُّ مِنْهَا وَأَطْلِعْهَا عَلَى أَمْرِكَ وَطِبْ نَفْسًا فَأَنْتَ آمِنٌ مِمَّا تَخَافُهُ مِنْ جِهَتِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-lā yakun ʿindaka aʿazzu minhā wa-aṭliʿhā ʿalā amrika wa-ṭib nafsan fa-anta āminun mimmā takhāfuhu min jihatinā
sentences.l: So let there not be with-you (one) dearer than-her; and inform-her of your-affair, and be-good as-to-soul, for you (are) safe from what you-fear-it from our-side.
sentences.i: So hold no one dearer than her: tell her all your business and set your mind at rest, for you have nothing to fear from us.
sentences.n: lā yakun, a prohibition with the jussive, “let there not be”; aʿazzu minhā, “dearer than her”, an elative with min, stands as its subject. ṭib nafsan, “be of good heart”: the imperative of ṭāba, “to be good”, with nafs as accusative of specification. mimmā is min mā, “from what”. The madda of آمن is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَمَا يُسَدُّ عَلَيْكَ مَوْضِعٌ إِلَّا وَتَفْتَحُهُ لَكَ وَهِيَ تَأْتِيكَ مِنْ عِنْدِي بِأَخْبَارِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ وَتَكُونُ أَنْتَ الْوَاسِطَةَ فِي التَّبْلِيغِ بَيْنَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-mā yusaddu ʿalayka mawḍiʿun illā wa-taftaḥuhu laka wa-hiya taʾtīka min ʿindī bi-akhbāri ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin wa-takūnu anta al-wāsiṭata fī al-tablīghi baynanā
sentences.l: For no place is-blocked against-you but she-opens-it for-you; and she will-come-to-you from with-me with the tidings of ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and you will-be the go-between in the conveying between-us.
sentences.i: No door will be shut against you but she will open it for you. She will bring you word from me touching ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and you shall be the go-between who carries our messages.”
sentences.n: mā … illā wa-, “not … but”: after a negative, illā followed by a circumstantial wa- introduces what happens in every case. yusaddu, passive of sadda, “to block, stop up”; its shadda is the print's own, as is the hamza of تأتيك. atā bi- is “to bring”, so taʾtīka … bi-akhbāri is “she will bring you tidings”; akhbār ʿAlī, “the tidings of ʿAlī”, are the messages that concern him. The print spells ʿindī with ي here, after عندى above. wāsiṭa, “intermediary, go-between”; tablīgh, “conveying (a message)”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ قَامَتْ وَهِيَ لَا تَسْتَطِيعُ الْقِيَامَ وَمَشَتْ فَتَمَشَّى بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا الْجَوْهَرِيُّ إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلَتْ إِلَى بَابِ الدَّارِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Shamsa al-Nahāri qāmat wa-hiya lā tastaṭīʿu al-qiyāma wa-mashat fa-tamashshā bayna yadayhā al-jawhariyyu ilā an waṣalat ilā bābi al-dāri
sentences.l: Then (indeed) Shams al-Nahār rose, she not being-able (for) the rising, and walked; and the jeweller walked between her-two-hands until she-reached the door of the house.
sentences.i: Then Shams al-Nahār rose, though she had hardly the strength to stand, and walked out, the jeweller going before her until she reached the door of the house.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then (it was that)”, is a narrative opener: inna only puts the subject in the accusative and is not translated. wa-hiya lā tastaṭīʿu, a circumstantial clause, “while she could not”. bayna yadayhā, “between her two hands”, means “in front of her”. tamashshā (Form V), “to walk along”, printed with final ى; ilā an, “until”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَجَعَ وَقَعَدَ فِى مَوْضِعِهِ بَعْدَ أَنْ نَظَرَ مِنْ حُسْنِهَا مَا بَهَرَهُ وَسَمِعَ مِنْ مَقَالِهَا مَا حَيَّرَ عَقْلَهُ وَشَاهَدَ مِنْ ظَرْفِهَا وَأَدَبِهَا مَا أَدْهَشَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma rajaʿa wa-qaʿada fī mawḍiʿihi baʿda an naẓara min ḥusnihā mā baharahu wa-samiʿa min maqālihā mā ḥayyara ʿaqlahu wa-shāhada min ẓarfihā wa-adabihā mā adhashahu
sentences.l: Then he-returned and sat in his-place, after he had-seen of her-beauty what dazzled-him, and heard of her-speech what bewildered his-mind, and witnessed of her-elegance and her-breeding what astounded-him.
sentences.i: Then he went back and sat down in his place, having seen in her a beauty that dazzled him, heard from her words that bewildered his mind, and witnessed a grace and breeding that left him amazed.
sentences.n: Three matching clauses, each min … mā, “of her … what”: min names the quality, mā what it did to him. bahara, “to dazzle, overwhelm”; ḥayyara (Form II), “to bewilder”; adhasha (Form IV), “to astonish”. ẓarf, “elegance, refinement”, and adab, “good breeding, cultivation”, are a common pair. فى is the print's spelling of fī.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اسْتَمَرَّ يَتَفَكَّرُ فِي شَمَائِلِهَا حَتَّى سَكَنَتْ نَفْسُهُ وَطَلَبَ الطَّعَامَ فَأَكَلَ مَا يُمْسِكُ رَمَقَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma istamarra yatafakkaru fī shamāʾilihā ḥattā sakanat nafsuhu wa-ṭalaba al-ṭaʿāma fa-akala mā yumsiku ramaqahu
sentences.l: Then he-continued pondering on her-qualities until his-soul grew-calm; and he-asked-for the food and ate what holds-fast his-last-breath.
sentences.i: He went on musing on her charms until his spirit grew calm. Then he called for food and ate just enough to keep himself alive.
sentences.n: istamarra (Form X), “to continue”, followed directly by an imperfect: “kept on thinking”; its shadda is the print's own. shamāʾil, “qualities, traits”, often of a person's charm; the ئ is printed. ramaq, “the last spark of life”: akala mā yumsiku ramaqahu, “he ate what would hold on to his last breath”, is a set phrase for eating barely enough to live.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ غَيَّرَ ثِيَابَهُ وَخَرَجَ مِنْ دَارِهِ وَتَوَجَّهَ إِلَى الْفَتَى عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ فَطَرَقَ بَابَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma ghayyara thiyābahu wa-kharaja min dārihi wa-tawajjaha ilā al-fatā ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin fa-ṭaraqa bābahu
sentences.l: Then he-changed his-clothes and went-out from his-house and turned toward the young-man ʿAlī son of Bakkār, and knocked-at his-door.
sentences.i: Then he changed his clothes, left his house, and made his way to young ʿAlī ibn Bakkār, and knocked at his door.
sentences.n: The print has نطرق, a misprint for فطرق, corrected here. ghayyara (Form II), “to change”; its shadda is the print's own. tawajjaha ilā (Form V), “to set out toward”. al-fatā, “the young man”, stands before the name in apposition.

sentences.t: فَمَا تَوَانَتْ غِلْمَانُهُ حَتَّى لَاقَوْهُ وَمَشَوْا أَمَامَهُ إِلَى أَنْ أَوْصَلُوهُ إِلَى سَيِّدِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-mā tawānat ghilmānuhu ḥattā lāqawhu wa-mashaw amāmahu ilā an awṣalūhu ilā sayyidihim
sentences.l: And his-pages did-not slacken until they-met-him, and walked before-him until they-brought-him to their-master.
sentences.i: His servants lost no time in coming to meet him, and walked ahead of him until they had brought him to their master.
sentences.n: tawānā (Form VI), “to be slow, slack”: mā tawānat … ḥattā, “they did not hang back until”, means they came at once. ghilmān, “pages, serving-boys”, a broken plural, takes a feminine singular verb here (tawānat) and then masculine plurals (lāqawhu, mashaw); both agreements are possible with plurals of persons. awṣala (Form IV), “to bring someone to”.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَهُ مُلْقًى عَلَى فِرَاشِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadahu mulqan ʿalā firāshihi
sentences.l: And he-found-him cast-down upon his-bed.
sentences.i: He found him lying prostrate on his bed.
sentences.n: mulqan, passive participle of alqā, “to throw”: “cast down, lying helpless”. The final ى is not sounded; the tanwīn falls on the qāf.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى الْجَوْهَرِيَّ قَالَ لَهُ أَبْطَأْتَ عَلَىَّ فَزِدْتَنِي هَمًّا عَلَي هَمِّي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā al-jawhariyya qāla lahu abṭaʾta ʿalayya fa-zidtanī hamman ʿalā hammī
sentences.l: And when he-saw the jeweller he-said to-him: You-were-slow upon-me, and you-increased-me worry upon my-worry.
sentences.i: When he saw the jeweller he said to him, “You have been long in coming, and have heaped worry on my worry.”
sentences.n: abṭaʾa ʿalā (Form IV), “to be slow in coming to someone”; the hamza of ابطأت and of رأى is printed. zāda, “to increase”, takes two objects: zidtanī hamman, “you increased me (in) worry”. The print spells the two ʿalās differently: علىّ, with the shadda on the ى, for ʿalayya, “to me”, and علي, with ي, for plain ʿalā, “upon”. The shaddas of همّا and همّي are the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَرَفَ غِلْمَانَهُ وَأَمَرَ بِغَلْقِ أَبْوَابِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣarafa ghilmānahu wa-amara bi-ghalqi abwābihi
sentences.l: Then he-dismissed his-pages and commanded the shutting of his-doors.
sentences.i: Then he sent his servants away and ordered his doors to be shut.
sentences.n: ṣarafa, “to send away, dismiss”. amara bi-, “to order (something)”: the verb takes the thing ordered through bi-. ghalq, “shutting”, is the verbal noun of ghalaqa; Classical prefers Form IV, aghlaqa, ighlāq.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ وَاللَّهِ يَا أَخِي مَا غَمَضَتْ عَيْنِي مِنْ يَوْمِ فَارَقْتَنِي فَإِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ جَاءَتْنِي بِالْأَمْسِ وَمَعَهَا رُقْعَةٌ مَخْتُومَةٌ مِنْ عِنْدِ سَيِّدَتِهَا شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu wa-Allāhi yā akhī mā ghamaḍat ʿaynī min yawmi fāraqtanī fa-inna al-jāriyata jāʾatnī bi-al-amsi wa-maʿahā ruqʿatun makhtūmatun min ʿindi sayyidatihā Shamsi al-Nahāri
sentences.l: And he-said to-him: By God, O my-brother, my-eye has-not closed from the day you-parted-from-me; for the slave-girl came-to-me yesterday, and with-her a sealed note from with her-mistress Shams al-Nahār.
sentences.i: And he said to him, “By God, my brother, I have not closed my eyes since the day you left me. Yesterday the slave-girl came to me, bringing a sealed note from her mistress Shams al-Nahār.”
sentences.n: The print has قان, a misprint for فان, corrected here. ghamaḍat ʿaynī, “my eye closed”: the verb is intransitive, with the eye as subject. min yawmi fāraqtanī, “from the day you left me”: yawm is put in construct directly before a verb, with no word for “that”. bi-al-amsi, “yesterday”, literally “in the yesterday”, bi- of time. min ʿindi, “from the presence of”, simply “from”.

sentences.t: وَحَكَى لَهُ ابْنُ بَكَّارٍ عَلَى جَمِيعِ مَا وَقَعَ لَهُ مَعَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ḥakā lahu Ibnu Bakkārin ʿalā jamīʿi mā waqaʿa lahu maʿahā
sentences.l: And Ibn Bakkār related to-him about all that befell him with-her.
sentences.i: And Ibn Bakkār told him everything that had passed between him and the girl.
sentences.n: ḥakā ʿalā, “to tell about”: Classical would make the matter the direct object (ḥakā lahu jamīʿa mā …); ʿalā in the sense “about, concerning” is a Middle Arabic habit of this text. waqaʿa lahu, “befell him”. Ibn Bakkār is ʿAlī, called by his father's name.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ وَاللَّهِ لَقَدْ تَحَيَّرْتُ فِي أَمْرِي وَقَلَّ صَبْرِي وَكَانَ لِي أَبُو الْحَسَنِ أَنِيسًا لِأَنَّهُ يَعْرِفُ الْجَارِيَةَ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla wa-Allāhi la-qad taḥayyartu fī amrī wa-qalla ṣabrī wa-kāna lī Abū al-Ḥasani anīsan li-annahu yaʿrifu al-jāriyata
sentences.l: Then he-said: By God, I have-indeed become-bewildered in my-affair, and my-patience has-grown-little; and Abū al-Ḥasan was to-me a-companion, because he knows the slave-girl.
sentences.i: Then he said, “By God, I am at my wits' end and my patience is wearing thin. Abū al-Ḥasan used to be my comfort, for he knew the slave-girl.”
sentences.n: la-qad after an oath, “indeed”, confirms the perfect. taḥayyara (Form V), “to be perplexed”. qalla ṣabrī, “my patience grew little”; the shadda of وقلّ is the print's own. kāna … anīsan, “was a companion”, predicate of kāna in the accusative; anīs is one whose company cheers. li-annahu, “because he”: li- of cause before anna. yaʿrifu is imperfect, “he knows”, describing how things stood.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ كَلَامَهُ ضَحِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-jawhariyyu kalāmahu ḍaḥika
sentences.l: And when the jeweller heard his words, he laughed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ ابْنُ بَكَّارٍ كَيْفَ تَضْحَكُ مِنْ كَلَامِي وَقَدِ اسْتَبْشَرْتُ بِكَ وَاتَّخَذْتُكَ عُدَّةً لِلنَّائِبَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Ibnu Bakkārin kayfa taḍḥaku min kalāmī wa-qadi istabshartu bika wa-ittakhadhtuka ʿuddatan li-al-nāʾibāti
sentences.l: And Ibn Bakkār said to-him: How do-you-laugh at my-words, when I-had-rejoiced in-you and taken-you (as) a-provision for the misfortunes?
sentences.i: Ibn Bakkār said to him, “How can you laugh at what I say, when I had taken heart from you and counted on you as my stand-by in time of trouble?”
sentences.n: ḍaḥika min, “to laugh at”: min marks what is laughed at. istabshara bi- (Form X), “to rejoice at, take as good news”, bi- marking the cause. ittakhadha (Form VIII) takes two objects, “to take someone as something”. ʿudda, “equipment, what is held ready”; li-al-nāʾibāt, “for the calamities”, li- of purpose; nāʾiba, “a mishap that befalls one”. The shadda of عدّة and the ئ of للنائبات are the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَأَوَّهَ وَبَكَي وَأَنْشَدَ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: thumma taʾawwaha wa-bakā wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: Then he-sighed and wept and recited these verses:
sentences.i: Then he sighed and wept, and recited these lines:
sentences.n: taʾawwaha (Form V), “to sigh, cry āh”; the print gives the shadda (تاوّه) but no hamza. bakā is printed بكي, with ي for ى, and read bakā.

sentences.t:
وَضَاحِكٍ مِنْ بُكَائِي حِينَ اَبْصَرَنِي * لَوْكَانَ قَاسَى الَّذِي قَاسَيْتُ اَبْكَاهُ
لَمْ يَرْثِ لِلْمُبْتَلِي مِمَّا يُكَابِدُهُ * اِلَّا شَجٍ مِثْلُهُ قَدْ طَالَ بَلْوَاهُ
وَجْدِي حَنِينِي اَنِينِي فِكْرَتِي وَلَهِي * اِلَى حَبِيبٍ زَوَايَا الْقَلْبِ مَأْوَاهُ
حَلَّ الْفُؤَادَ مُقِيمًا لَا يُفَارِقُهُ * وَقْتًا وَلَكِنَّهُ قَدْ عَزَّ لُقْيَاهُ
مَالِيْ سِوَاهُ خَلِيلٌ اَرْتَضِي بَدَلًا * وَمَا اصْطَفَيْتُ حَبِيبًا قَطُّ اِلَّا هُوَ
sentences.tr:
wa-ḍāḥikin min bukāʾī ḥīna abṣaranī * law kāna qāsā alladhī qāsaytu abkāhu
lam yarthi li-al-mubtalī mimmā yukābiduhu * illā shajin mithluhu qad ṭāla balwāhu
wajdī ḥanīnī anīnī fikratī walahī * ilā ḥabībin zawāyā al-qalbi maʾwāhu
ḥalla al-fuʾāda muqīman lā yufāriquhu * waqtan wa-lākinnahu qad ʿazza luqyāhu
mā lī siwāhu khalīlun artaḍī badalan * wa-mā iṣṭafaytu ḥabīban qaṭṭu illā huwa
sentences.l:
And (many) a one-laughing at my-weeping when he-saw-me — * if he-had suffered what I-have-suffered, it-would-have-made-him-weep;
he-does-not pity the afflicted-one for what he-endures * except a grief-stricken-one like-him, whose affliction has-grown-long.
My-passion, my-longing, my-moaning, my-brooding, my-distraction * (are) toward a beloved: the corners of the heart (are) his-shelter.
He-has-settled-in the heart, abiding, not leaving-it * a moment; but-he — meeting-him has-grown-hard.
There-is-not to-me besides-him a friend I-would-accept as-substitute, * and I-have-not chosen a beloved ever except he.
sentences.i:
Many a one who laughs to see me weep — had he suffered what I have suffered, he would weep too;
none pities the afflicted for what he bears but one as stricken, whose own affliction has been long.
My passion, my longing, my moaning, my brooding and my distraction are all for a beloved who dwells in the heart's inmost corners.
He has made the heart his home and never leaves it for a moment; and yet to meet him has grown hard.
I have no friend besides him whom I would take in his place, and I have never chosen any beloved but him.
sentences.n: Metre: basīṭ, rhyming in -āhu. The pointing is the print's own, kept as printed, including the bare alif of اَبْصَرَنِي, اَبْكَاهُ and اِلَّا where the edition marks no hamza. The opening wa- is the “wāw of rubba”, “many a …”, which puts its noun in the genitive: ḍāḥikin. The print sets law kāna as one word (لَوْكَانَ) and mā lī likewise (مَالِيْ, with its usual sukūn on the long vowel). qāsā (Form III), “to suffer, endure”, comes twice, then abkāhu, “it would have made him weep” (Form IV of bakā); a law-condition can take its answer without la-. rathā li-, “to pity”: li- marks the one pitied; yarthi is jussive after lam. shajin is shajī, “grief-stricken”, whose final -ī drops before the tanwīn. balwā, “affliction”, is feminine in form, yet ṭāla is masculine: allowed when the verb comes first and the noun is not a living female. Line 3 strings five nouns, each with -ī “my”, and no “and” between them. zawāyā is the plural of zāwiya, “corner”; maʾwā, “shelter, abode”. ʿazza, “to be rare, hard to come by”; luqyā, “meeting”. The beloved is “he” throughout, the usual convention of love poetry even when the beloved is a woman, as here. The last line ends illā huwa: after a verb with an object, Classical grammar wants illā iyyāhu, “but him”, which would also keep the -āhu rhyme; the print's huwa breaks both, and may be a slip.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ مِنْهُ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ وَفَهِمَ الشِّعْرَ وَالنِّظَامَ بَكَى لِبُكَائِهِ وَأَخْبَرَهُ بِمَا جَرَى لَهُ مَعَ الْجَارِيَةِ وَسَيِّدَتِهَا مِنْ حِينِ فَارَقَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-jawhariyyu minhu hādhā al-kalāma wa-fahima al-shiʿra wa-al-niẓāma bakā li-bukāʾihi wa-akhbarahu bi-mā jarā lahu maʿa al-jāriyati wa-sayyidatihā min ḥīni fāraqahu
sentences.l: And when the jeweller heard from-him this speech, and understood the poetry and the arrangement, he-wept at his-weeping; and he-told-him of what had-happened to-him with the slave-girl and her-mistress from the time he-parted-from-him.
sentences.i: When the jeweller heard these words from him and understood the poem and its craft, he wept to see him weep, and told him all that had passed between himself and the slave-girl and her mistress since he had left him.
sentences.n: The rhyme of al-kalām and al-niẓām is sajʿ. niẓām, “arrangement, stringing (of pearls)”, is used of the composing of verse. li-bukāʾihi: li- gives the cause, “because of his weeping”; the hamza (ئ) is the print's own. akhbara bi-, “to tell of”, bi- marking what is told. jarā li-, “to happen to”. min ḥīni fāraqahu, “from the time he left him”: ḥīn stands in construct with a whole verbal clause.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ ابْنُ بَكَّارٍ يُصْغِي إِلَى كَلَامِهِ وَكُلَّمَا سَمِعَ مِنْهُ كَلِمَةً يَتَغَيَّرُ لَوْنُ وَجْهِهِ مِنْ صُفْرَةٍ إِلَى احْمِرَارٍ وَيَقْوَي جِسْمُهُ مَرَّةً وَيَضْعُفُ أُخْرَى
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra Ibnu Bakkārin yuṣghī ilā kalāmihi wa-kullamā samiʿa minhu kalimatan yataghayyaru lawnu wajhihi min ṣufratin ilā iḥmirārin wa-yaqwā jismuhu marratan wa-yaḍʿufu ukhrā
sentences.l: And Ibn Bakkār began listening to his-speech; and whenever he-heard from-him a word, the colour of his-face changes from yellowness to redness, and his-body grows-strong one-time and grows-weak another.
sentences.i: Ibn Bakkār listened intently to what he said, and at every word he heard the colour of his face would change from yellow to red; one moment his body would gather strength, and the next it would fail.
sentences.n: The print has منة, a misprint for منه, corrected here. The print has يضغف, a misprint for يضعف, corrected here. ṣāra with an imperfect, “he began to, he went on”. aṣghā ilā (Form IV), “to lend an ear to, listen to”. kullamā, “whenever”, here with an imperfect in the main clause (yataghayyaru), describing what kept happening; Classical narrative would more often use the perfect. Yellow is the colour of the lovesick and fearful, red of the flushed and hopeful. yaqwā, “grows strong”, is spelt with a dotted yāʾ (يقوي) for the final alif maqṣūra, as the print often does with ilā (الي). marratan … ukhrā, “one time … another”. The shadda of يتغيّر is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا انْتَهَى إِلَى آخِرِ الْكَلَامِ بَكَى ابْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا أَخِي أَنَا عَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ هَالِكٌ فَلَيْتَ أَجَلِي قَرِيبٌ كُنْتُ أَرْتَاحُ مِنْ هَذَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā intahā ilā ākhiri al-kalāmi bakā Ibnu Bakkārin wa-qāla lahu yā akhī anā ʿalā kulli ḥālin hālikun fa-layta ajalī qarībun kuntu artāḥu min hādhā
sentences.l: And when he-came-to-the-end at the last of the speech, Ibn Bakkār wept and said to-him: O my-brother, I (am) in every state perishing; and would-that my-appointed-term (were) near — I-would-be resting from this.
sentences.i: When the jeweller came to the end of his account, Ibn Bakkār wept and said to him, “My brother, whatever happens I am a dead man. If only my hour were near, I would be at rest from all this.
sentences.n: intahā ilā (Form VIII), “to come to the end at, reach”; the subject is the jeweller. ʿalā kulli ḥālin, “in any case, whatever happens”. hālik, “perishing, doomed”. ajal is the term of life God has fixed. layta, “would that”, takes ajalī as its noun and qarībun as its predicate. kuntu artāḥu, “I would be resting”, is Middle Arabic: kāna with an imperfect, standing as the answer to the wish with no linking word, where Classical would build a proper condition. irtāḥa min (Form VIII), “to find rest from, be relieved of”. The madda of آخر is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ أَنْ تَكُونَ مُعَاوِنِي وَمُلَاطِفِي فِي جَمِيعِ أُمُورِي إِلَى أَنْ يُرِيدَ اللَّهُ بِمَا يُرِيدُهُ وَإِنِّي لَاأُخَالِفُ لَكَ قَوْلًا
sentences.tr: wa-lākinnī asʾaluka min faḍlika an takūna muʿāwinī wa-mulāṭifī fī jamīʿi umūrī ilā an yurīda Allāhu bi-mā yurīduhu wa-innī lā ukhālifu laka qawlan
sentences.l: But-I ask-you of your-bounty that you-be my-helper and my-kind-one in all my-affairs, until God wills with what He-wills; and indeed-I will-not go-against for-you a word.
sentences.i: But I ask you, of your kindness, to stand by me and deal gently with me in all my affairs, until God brings about whatever He wills; and I will not go against a single word of yours.”
sentences.n: min faḍlika, “of your bounty”, i.e. “please, as a favour”. muʿāwin (Form III participle), “helper”; mulāṭif, “one who treats kindly, comforts” (Form III of laṭufa). arāda normally takes its object directly; here bi-mā, “with what”, is unusual: Classical uses arāda bi- for the person something is meant for (arāda bihi khayran, “he intended good for him”), not for the thing willed; the sense is “until God brings about what He wills”. khālafa, “to oppose, disobey”, also takes a direct object in Classical; laka, “for you”, makes the word yours: “I will not go against a word of yours”. The print sets lā ukhālifu as one word (لااخالف).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ لَا يُطْفِئُ عَنْكَ هَذِهِ النَّارَ إِلَّا الِاجْتِمَاعُ بِمَنْ شُغِفْتَ بِهَا وَلَكِنْ يَكُونُ فِي غَيْرِ هَذَا الْمَكَانِ الْخَطِيرِ بَلْ يَكُونُ ذَلِكَ عِنْدِي فِى الْمَوْضِعِ الَّذِي جَاءَتْنِي فِيهِ الْجَارِيَةُ وَسَيِّدَتُهَا وَهُوَ الْمَوْضِعُ الَّذِي اخْتَارَتْهُ لِنَفْسِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-jawhariyyu lā yuṭfiʾu ʿanka hādhihi al-nāra illā al-ijtimāʿu bi-man shughifta bihā wa-lākin yakūnu fī ghayri hādhā al-makāni al-khaṭīri bal yakūnu dhālika ʿindī fī al-mawḍiʿi alladhī jāʾatnī fīhi al-jāriyatu wa-sayyidatuhā wa-huwa al-mawḍiʿu alladhī ikhtārathu li-nafsihā
sentences.l: And the jeweller said to-him: Nothing puts-out from-you this fire except the meeting with (her) whom you-have-been-smitten with-her; but it-shall-be in other-than this perilous place; rather that shall-be at-me, in the spot in-which the slave-girl and her-mistress came-to-me, and it (is) the spot which she-chose for herself.
sentences.i: The jeweller said to him, “Nothing will put out this fire in you but being with the woman you have lost your heart to. Only it must not be in this perilous place; it shall be at my house, in the place where the slave-girl and her mistress came to me, the place she chose for herself.
sentences.n: aṭfaʾa (Form IV), “to put out, quench”; the hamza (ئ) of يطفئ is the print's own. ʿanka, “from you, off you”. al-ijtimāʿ bi-, “meeting with”, bi- marking the person met. shughifa bi- (passive), “to be smitten with love for”, bi- marking the one loved; man, “the one who”, takes the feminine pronoun bihā because a woman is meant. al-khaṭīr, “dangerous, perilous”: a meeting at ʿAlī's own house could be found out. ʿindī, “at my place”. The woman who chose the place is Shams al-Nahār. فى is the print's spelling of fī, beside في in the same sentence.

sentences.t: وَالْمَقْصُودُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ اجْتِمَاعُكُمَا بِبَعْضِكُمَا وَشَكْوَاكُمَا مَا قَاسَيْتُمَا مِنْ أَلَمِ الْحُبِّ
sentences.tr: wa-al-maqṣūdu min dhālika ijtimāʿukumā bi-baʿḍikumā wa-shakwākumā mā qāsaytumā min alami al-ḥubbi
sentences.l: And the intended (thing) from that (is) your-two meeting with some-of-you-two, and your-two complaining (of) what you-two-have-suffered of the pain of love.
sentences.i: The point of it is that the two of you should meet and pour out to each other all you have suffered from the pain of love.”
sentences.n: -kumā, “you two, your (two)”, the dual pronoun. ijtimāʿukumā bi-baʿḍikumā, “your meeting with one another”: a loose reciprocal with baʿḍ alone, where Classical would say baʿḍikumā bi-baʿḍin. shakwā, “complaint”, a verbal noun that here takes its object directly: “your complaining (of) what you have suffered”. qāsā (Form III), “to suffer”, the verb of the poem.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ يَا سَيِّدِي افْعَلْ مَا تُرِيدُ وَأَجْرُكَ عَلَى اللَّهِ فَمَاتَرَى فِيهِ الصَّوَابَ عَلَيْكَ بِهِ وَلَا تُطَوِّلْ عَلَيَّ لِئَلَّا أَمُوتَ بِهَذِهِ الْغُصَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin yā sayyidī ifʿal mā turīdu wa-ajruka ʿalā Allāhi fa-mā tarā fīhi al-ṣawāba ʿalayka bihi wa-lā tuṭawwil ʿalayya li-allā amūta bi-hādhihi al-ghuṣṣati
sentences.l: And ʿAlī son of Bakkār said: O my-lord, do what you-want, and your-reward (is) upon God; so what you-see in-it (to be) the right — upon-you with-it! And do-not make-it-long upon-me, lest I-die by this choking-grief.
sentences.i: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār said, “Sir, do what you will, and God will reward you. Whatever you judge right in this, hold to it; and do not keep me waiting long, or I shall die of this anguish.”
sentences.n: ajruka ʿalā Allāhi, “your reward rests with God”, a set phrase of thanks. mā tarā fīhi al-ṣawāba, “what you see to be the right course in it”: raʾā, “to deem”, takes al-ṣawāb as a second object. ʿalayka bihi, “hold to it, do it”: ʿalayka bi- is a fixed command, bi- marking what is to be done. The print runs fa-mā tarā together (فماترى). ṭawwala ʿalā (Form II), “to keep someone waiting long”; tuṭawwil is jussive after the prohibitive lā. li-allā, “so that … not, lest”, is li- + an + lā. ghuṣṣa, “something stuck in the throat”, hence choking grief; bi- gives the cause. The shadda of عليّ and the hamza of لئلا are the print's own.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَأَقَمْتُ عِنْدَهُ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ أُسَامِرُهُ إِلَى أَنْ أَصْبَحَ الصَّبَاحُ وَطَلَعَ النَّهَارُ
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-aqamtu ʿindahu tilka al-laylata usāmiruhu ilā an aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu wa-ṭalaʿa al-nahāru
sentences.l: The jeweller said: And I-stayed with-him that night, talking-by-night-with-him, until the morning became-morning and the day rose.
sentences.i: The jeweller said: So I stayed with him that night, keeping him company in talk, until morning came and the day broke.
sentences.n: Here the jeweller takes over the telling in his own voice, “I stayed”, and his account runs on inside Shahrazād's. aqāma (Form IV), “to stay, remain”. sāmara (Form III), “to keep someone company in talk by night”, from samar, “night conversation”. aṣbaḥa al-ṣabāḥu, “the morning dawned”, verb and subject from the same root.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
